claims.text: Superconducting transition temperature in the proposed non-Nb-Ta, non-titanium-rich single-phase HEA is primarily governed by lattice distortion arising from atomic-size mismatch.
Increasing atomic-size variance increases lattice distortion.
Increasing atomic-size variance enhances electron scattering.
Enhanced electron scattering reduces the effective electron-phonon coupling strength.
Reduced effective electron-phonon coupling lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
The starting material is a superconducting, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each.
The starting material has a BCC or similar structure with relatively low atomic-size variance.
Substituting an element with one of significantly different atomic radius can increase atomic-size variance without introducing secondary phases.
Lattice distortion acts as scattering centers that disrupt Cooper-pair formation.
Disorder-induced electron scattering reduces the electron mean free path.
Electron-phonon coupling is the principal Cooper-pair formation mechanism in conventional superconductors.
An alloy with lower lattice distortion has a cleaner electronic environment and a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Relative to the low-distortion baseline, the higher-size-mismatch alloy will show a measurable decrease in superconducting transition temperature.
The predicted superconducting transition-temperature reduction is approximately 5–10%.

The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and valence electron count, magnetic ordering, phase separation, pressure, and processing effects are controlled.
Direct prior evidence connecting atomic-size-mismatch lattice distortion to superconducting transition temperature in HEAs outside Nb-Ta or titanium-rich systems is limited.

contradictions.description: The intervention explicitly modifies composition by substituting an element, whereas the experiment calls for samples with identical overall compositions that differ in atomic-size variance. Elemental substitution necessarily changes composition, so these requirements cannot both hold literally.
The design internally requests identical overall compositions while also specifying elemental substitution as the means of producing different size mismatch.
